extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, teachers, and editors seeking guidance on clear prose
extracted.subtask_description: A general prose style guide presenting numbered rules and usage notes for clear, concise, and effective English prose—covering sentence construction, emphasis, concreteness, punctuation, form, and commonly misused words and expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express negatives in positive form
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, it is better to express even a negative in positive form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'not honest' → 'dishonest'; 'did not remember' → 'forgot'. The antithesis of negative and positive is strong (e.g., 'Not charity, but simple justice'). Note that negative words other than 'not' are usually strong ('The sun never sets upon the British flag'). Prefer positive constructions for force and concision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definite, specific, concrete language
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the specific to the general, the definite to the vague, the concrete to the abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give significant details (not every detail) with sufficient definiteness that the reader can project into the scene. Use concrete examples in exposition and argument; when dealing with general principles give particular instances of application. Specific terms produce immediate images and economy of expression (Herbert Spencer examples; literary examples from Browning, Ruskin, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit needless words
rubrics_metrics.description: Vigorous writing is concise; a sentence should contain no unnecessary words and a paragraph no unnecessary sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make every word tell. Avoid filler phrases ('the question whether', 'no doubt', 'used for fuel purposes', 'in a hasty manner', 'the fact that') and unnecessary copula constructions ('he is a man who…'). Active voice and positive statements are often more concise than negatives and passives. Combine a series of short, step-by-step sentences into a single clear sentence where appropriate; examples contrast word counts of verbose vs concise rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a succession of loose sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid writing a series of sentences that are mechanically similar loose sentences (two co-ordinate clauses often joined by 'and', 'but', 'so').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A paragraph composed of such similar sentences becomes monotonous and tedious. Recast some sentences to produce variety: use simple sentences, semi-colons, periodic sentences, or sentences of three clauses to represent true relations of thought. Compare with stronger prose (examples given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Express co-ordinate ideas in similar form (parallel construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of similar content and function should be outwardly similar (parallel construction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallel form makes likeness of content/function clearer. Correlative expressions (both…and; not only…but also; either…or; first, second, third; etc.) should be followed by the same grammatical construction. Avoid faulty arrangement that breaks parallelism. If many similar ideas exist, group them or use tables rather than forcing twenty identical sentence patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep related words together
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring together words or groups of words that are related in thought; keep apart those not so related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not separate subject and principal verb by transferable phrases or clauses. Place modifiers next to the words they modify; arrange multiple modifiers to avoid wrong relations; relative pronoun should generally follow its antecedent or the whole antecedent group; apposition may be an exception. Examples show recasting for clarity ('He found only two mistakes' vs 'He only found two mistakes').

rubrics_metrics.name: In summaries, keep to one tense
rubrics_metrics.description: When summarizing drama use the present tense; when summarizing poem, story, or novel prefer the present (past acceptable). Maintain a single tense throughout the summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using present tense, express antecedent action with the perfect; if past, use the past perfect. Do not shift tenses (appears as uncertainty). Avoid intercalating phrases like 'he said' repeatedly—indicate at the outset that what follows is summary and then proceed. In criticism/interpretation avoid falling into mere summary; aim for orderly discussion supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the emphatic words of a sentence at the end
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper place for the words the writer desires to make most prominent is usually the end of the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The logical predicate or the new element should often come at the end (periodic sentence gives prominence). The beginning of the sentence can also impart emphasis to non-subject elements. The same principle applies to sentences within paragraphs and paragraphs within a composition. Examples illustrate reordering to emphasize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headings: spacing and page starts
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave a blank line (or equivalent space) after the title or heading of a manuscript; on succeeding pages (if using ruled paper) begin on the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple formatting rule for manuscript readability and consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerals: use figures for dates and serial numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not spell out dates or other serial numbers; write them in figures or Roman notation as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'August 9, 1918' or '9 August 1918'; 'Chapter XII', 'Rule 3', '352nd Infantry'. Follow conventional forms appropriate to context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence containing a parenthetical expression is punctuated, outside the parentheses, as if the parenthetical were absent; the parenthetical itself is punctuated as if standing alone except omit the final stop unless it is ? or !.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I went to his house yesterday (my third attempt to see him), but he had left town.' If a wholly detached expression or sentence is parenthesized, the final stop comes before the closing parenthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations: punctuation and formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal quotations cited as documentary evidence are introduced by a colon and enclosed in quotation marks; quotations in apposition or as direct objects are preceded by a comma and enclosed in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long verse lines or multi-line quotations begin on a fresh line and are centered and need not be enclosed in quotation marks. Quotations introduced by 'that' are treated as indirect discourse and not enclosed. Proverbial expressions, familiar phrases of literary origin, colloquialisms, and slang generally require no quotation marks. Examples given (Constitution, La Rochefoucauld, Aristotle, Wordsworth, Keats).

rubrics_metrics.name: References: scholarly referencing practice
rubrics_metrics.description: In scholarly work abbreviate frequently occurring titles and give full forms in an alphabetical list at the end; give references in parenthesis or footnotes rather than in the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit words act, scene, line, book, volume, page except when referring by only one of them. Punctuate references as indicated (examples for plays and biblical refs provided). Put insertions like 'iii.ii' in parenthesis at the proper place in the sentence when referring to scenes/acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllabication: principles for dividing words
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line cannot hold a whole word but can hold one or more syllables, divide the word according to common principles; no absolute rule covers all cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles: (a) divide according to formation (know-ledge, Shake-speare); (b) divide on the vowel (edi-ble, propo-sition); (c) divide between double letters unless they are at the end of simple form (Appen-nines, Cincin-nati, refer-ring); (d) do not divide before final -ed if the e is silent (treat-ed but not roam-ed). Examples show consonant combinations and recommended divisions; students should consult printed books for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of literary works: typographic convention
rubrics_metrics.description: For titles of literary works scholarly usage prefers italics with capitalized initials; usage varies among editors and publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use italics (indicate by underscoring in manuscript), except when writing for a periodical that follows a different practice. Omit initial 'A' or 'The' from titles when placing the possessive before them (e.g., Dickens's Tale of Two Cities). Examples: The Iliad; As You Like It; A Tale of Two Cities; To a Skylark.

rubrics_metrics.name: All right (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'All right' is idiomatic in familiar speech as a detached phrase meaning 'Agreed' or 'Go ahead'; it is always written as two words and should be avoided in other uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatment note in 'Words and expressions commonly misused'—distinguish appropriate familiar uses from formal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: As good or better than (avoid awkward comparative phrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions like 'as good or better than' should be corrected by rearranging the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'My opinion is as good or better than his.' → 'My opinion is as good as his, or better (if not better).'

rubrics_metrics.name: As to whether (use 'whether')
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Whether' is sufficient; avoid the redundant phrase 'as to whether'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplify constructions by using 'whether' alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bid (verb usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Bid' takes the infinitive without 'to'; the past tense in the sense 'ordered' is 'bade'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usage note for correct verb complementation and past tense form.

rubrics_metrics.name: But (avoid unnecessary 'but' after certain words)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'But' is unnecessary after 'doubt' and 'help' and its too-frequent use can produce loose sentences and awkward contrasts following contrasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions like 'I have no doubt but that' (use 'I have no doubt that') or 'He could not help but see' (use 'He could not help seeing'). Recast sentences to avoid chaining contrasts and reservations (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Can vs may (modal distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Can' means 'am/is/are able' and should not be used as a substitute for 'may'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'may' to express permission or possibility when appropriate; reserve 'can' for ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case (avoid 'case' as unnecessary wordiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The noun 'case' is often unnecessary and redundant in many common phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'It has rarely been the case that…' with a simpler phrasing such as 'Few mistakes have been made.' See referenced works for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainly (avoid indiscriminate intensifier)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Certainly' is used indiscriminately by some writers as 'very' or to intensify any statement; avoid this mannerism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overuse is a mannerism bad in speech and worse in writing; prefer precise qualifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (avoid redundant use)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Character' is often redundant in phrases like 'acts of a hostile character' where 'hostile acts' suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer more direct, concise formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim (verb)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Claim' with an object-noun means 'lay claim to' and may be used with a dependent clause if this sense is clearly involved; it should not be used as a substitute for 'declare', 'maintain', or 'charge'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'claimed to be' rather than 'claimed that' when possible; choose more precise verbs for assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clever (avoid overuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Clever' has been greatly overused; best restricted to ingenuity displayed in small matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose more precise descriptors for notable qualities rather than defaulting to 'clever'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare: to vs with
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Compare to' points out resemblances between objects of different order (analogy); 'compare with' points out differences between objects of the same order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'compare to' for analogy (life compared to a pilgrimage); use 'compare with' for comparative analysis (Congress compared with the British Parliament). Provide examples to show distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider (avoid 'as' when meaning 'believe to be')
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'consider' means 'believe to be', it is not followed by 'as'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I consider him thoroughly competent' (not 'I consider him as thoroughly competent'). When 'considered' means 'examined' or 'discussed', 'as' may follow (e.g., 'considered Cromwell first as soldier and second as administrator').

rubrics_metrics.name: Data (treat as plural)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Data' is a plural noun (like 'phenomena' and 'strata').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plural agreement: 'These data were tabulated.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependable (prefer reliable/trustworthy)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Dependable' is a needless substitute for 'reliable' or 'trustworthy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the more idiomatic choice in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different than (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Different than' is not permissible; substitute 'different from', 'other than', or 'unlike'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the grammatically standard preposition in comparative contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divided into vs composed of
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Divided into' should not be misused for 'composed of'—the line can be subtle (e.g., plays divided into acts; poems composed of stanzas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term appropriate to the structural sense intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't (contraction usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Don't' is the contraction of 'do not'; the contraction of 'does not' is 'doesn't'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usage reminder on correct contractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due to (correct and incorrect uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Due to' is incorrect when used adverbially for 'through', 'because of', or 'owing to' (e.g., 'He lost the first game, due to carelessness' is wrong).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'due to' only when the phrase is predicative or modifies a particular noun ('This invention is due to Edison'; 'losses due to preventable fires').

rubrics_metrics.name: Folk (use singular collective)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Folk' is a collective noun equivalent to 'people'; use the singular form only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'folk' as singular in agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect vs affect (and vague 'effect' uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a noun 'effect' means result; as a verb it means to bring about or accomplish. Do not confuse with 'affect' (to influence). Avoid vague perfunctory uses of 'effect' in discussing arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer specific wording when describing artistic qualities rather than resorting to vague 'effects' (examples of weak usages given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Etc. (limit use)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Etc.' is equivalent to 'and the rest' and should not be used if one of 'and the rest', 'and so forth' would be insufficient—that is, if important particulars would be left in doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Least objectionable when it represents the last terms of a list already given in full or immaterial words at the end of a quotation. Incorrect at the end of a list introduced by phrases like 'such as' or 'for example.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (use for verifiable matters only)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Fact' should be used only of matters capable of direct verification, not matters of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: particular events or physical properties are facts; evaluative conclusions (e.g., 'Napoleon was the greatest') are not 'facts'. See guidance under 'the fact that'. Recast sentences to avoid the clumsy formula 'the fact that'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (avoid hackneyed use)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Factor' is a hackneyed word and its phrases can usually be replaced by something more direct and idiomatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'His superior training was the great factor in his winning the match' → 'He won the match by being better trained.' Avoid lazy abstract nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature (avoid hackneyed/empty use)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Feature' is another hackneyed word that usually adds nothing to the sentence; as a verb in the advertising sense (to offer as a special attraction) it should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either name what the feature is or describe it; avoid using 'feature' as filler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix (avoid colloquial uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Fix' colloquial in America for 'arrange', 'prepare', 'mend'—in writing restrict it to its literary senses (fasten, make firm, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use more formal verbs in prose rather than American colloquial 'fix'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get / have got (avoid colloquial 'have got')
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Get' as colloquial 'have got' for 'have' should not be used in formal writing; the preferable participle is 'got'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid colloquial 'have got' constructions; prefer 'have' or 'got' appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'He is a man who...' (avoid redundancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases of the type 'He is a man who is very ambitious' are redundant and wordy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast to eliminate unnecessary relative clauses: 'He is very ambitious.' or restructure sentence for concision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help (avoid unnecessary 'help' + 'but')
rubrics_metrics.description: See the treatment under 'But'—avoid constructions that use 'help' followed by 'but' redundantly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'could not help seeing' rather than 'could not help but see'.

rubrics_metrics.name: However (placement and meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'however' means 'nevertheless' it should not come first in its sentence or clause; when it comes first it means 'in whatever way' or 'to whatever extent'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct: 'The roads were almost impassable. At last, however, we succeeded.' Incorrect: 'However, we at last succeeded' (when meaning nevertheless). When first, use examples like 'However you advise him...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interesting (avoid as perfunctory label)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'interesting' as a perfunctory announcement that what follows will be interesting; instead, make it so by presenting the material directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not preface anecdotes or facts with 'An interesting story is told of…'—tell the story without preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kind of / sort of (restrict use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'kind of' as a substitute for 'rather' (before adjectives and verbs) or for 'something like' (before nouns) except in familiar style; restrict it to its literal sense (a kind of fossil resin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise modifiers in formal prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less vs fewer (quantity vs number)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Less' should not be misused for 'fewer'—'less' refers to quantity, 'fewer' to number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'fewer' with countable nouns ('fewer men'). Exception: 'The signers were less than a hundred' where 'less' is acceptable with a round collective number. Provide examples contrasting correct/incorrect usages.
